newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plane unharmed by possible shots in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plane unharmed by possible shots in Zaire.

text.p: The crew of an unarmed U.S. Navy patrol plane flying over Zaire saw possible anti-aircraft fire on Wednesday but the shooting was not confirmed and the plane was not damaged, the Pentagon said.

Navy Cmdr. Joe March, a Defence Department spokesman, said what might have been eight air bursts of shells from anti-aircraft guns were spotted one or two miles (1.6-3.2 km) from the P-3 Orion aircraft. The plane was flying south of Goma, Zaire, well above the range of anti-aircraft guns, he said.

The U.S. military has based two of the four-engine turboprop planes at Entebbe airport in neighbouring Uganda and is using the Orions, designed to hunt submarines, to search for thousands of refugees displaced from camps in Zaire.

The United States on Wednesday continued to formulate plans for expected participation in a Canadian-led military relief effort for tens of thousands of the refugees who have returned to Rwanda from Zaire in recent days. Many more thousands are believed to be still in Zaire.
March told Reuters the crew of the Orion spotted what might have been anti-aircraft fire up to two miles (3.2 km) away and several thousand feet (about 1,000 metres) below the plane.

"Crewmembers reported seeing approximately eight bursts, which appeared to be anti-aircraft rounds and not small arms fire. The type of weapon used on the ground is undetermined," March told Reuters. "After the incident, the aircraft departed the area and continued on its mission," he said.
The United States on Tuesday put off plans to send combat troops to Zaire and prepared instead for a military air relief operation into Rwanda to help half a million refugees there.

Defence Secretary William Perry said the return of some 500,000 people from Zaire to Rwanda had changed the situation and fewer than 1,000 U.S. "logistical" personnel were now needed for a military operation in Rwanda led by Canada.
Under the new plan about 200 U.S. Air Force personnel will be sent to Kigali airport in Rwanda, 500 to Entebbe and 100 to Mombasa in Kenya to prepare for the air relief operation.

Canada, which is leading the multinational military effort to ease the plight of the Rwandan refugees, put the international military relief operation on hold on Tuesday pending meetings this week with other countries involved.

The Pentagon stressed that President Bill Clinton, while agreeing to U.S. participation in principle, had still not given final approval for the actual mission, which could change in response to circumstances on the ground.
